The end goal of fixing the broken immigration system is no one should ever be illegal at all times, i.e., the penalties for being here or employing an illegal alien should be so harsh that no one ever risks it.

One way to deal with this is to have a very simple high volume migrant program, with relatively little paperwork.  Want to become an economic migrant in the US?  Show up at a port of entry, provide identification and intended destination.  Receive a phone number to call, or website or physical location to visit for routine check-ins.  The program has a massive number of slots, like 5 million.  Almost everyone who shows up gets in (still allows for basic screening like terrorist/gang watch lists.

Here are the rules:

1) You have to checkin at a fixed rate, like every month.  Miss a checkin by more than two weeks and you become instantly deportable, no questions asked
2) A continued papers check continues on you while you are here and you must supply any needed documentation on a timely manner.
3) You have to be paid minimum wage and all labor laws apply to your employer
4) You have to remain within your stated location.  You can apply to change location, but that has to be approved.
5) You can vacation within the US, just don't miss your checkin.
6) You have to stay employed.  Even short term contractor work is OK for this.  Once you've been unemployed long enough, you have to go back to your home country.
7) If you have children, they are not automatically granted citizenship unless the other parent is a US citizen (I am fully aware this requires a constitutional amendment)
8) This is the kicker.  You cannot stay longer than some fixed time period, like 2-3 years.  You have to return to either your home country or a different country for at least 6 months to a year before you can reapply.
9) Conviction of any serious crime will result in immediate removal after time served.  Any minor criminal record in the US , will prevent future entries from this program for some number of years, like 5-10 years.  Any major criminal record is a permanent ban.
10) Current migrants are grandfathered in automatically, which means all illegal aliens who have been in the US for decades would have to leave within 2-3 years.  Obviously, this raises the allowed number for the first few years by default.  Anyone who avoids this for too long becomes instantly deportable.
11) Companies can apply to convert workers longer term migrant statuses.  This will be easily abused, so has to be significantly limited in number and requires competent oversight.
12) The asylum system can be absorbed into this, where an asylum claim can be processed during check-ins.  

There are probably lots of variations on this that could be possible.  The point is it allows a lot of migrants into the country which helps us and them economically.  It removes the illegal nature of it, provides incentives to encourage staying in the system.

This isn't meant to be an implement-tomorrow plan.  It probably requires too many constitutional amendments and at least one of our political parties to convert to being common sense based.  It's more of a blueprint for a way to handle the too-large number of illegals while also dealing with the economic fallout.

The end goal of fixing the broken healthcare system is that no one should ever go bankrupt or die because they can't afford care, i.e., the incentives for insurers to deny coverage and gouge patients should be so thoroughly dismantled that no corporation ever risks it.

One way to deal with this is to have a very simple high-volume public option program, with relatively little bureaucratic overhead. Want to enroll in affordable healthcare in the US? Show up at a enrollment center or go online, provide basic income information and your county of residence. Receive a coverage card and a straightforward portal for annual renewals. The program has a massive number of slots, like 50 million. Almost everyone who applies gets covered (still allows for basic verification like fraud screening).

Here are the rules:

1) You have to renew at a fixed rate, like every year. Miss a renewal by more than a month and your subsidy tier gets reassessed, no exceptions.
2) A continued income verification continues on you while enrolled and you must supply any needed documentation in a timely manner.
3) Insurers must cover all medically necessary procedures and all consumer protection laws apply to your provider.
4) You have to remain within your stated coverage network. You can apply to change networks, but that has to be approved.
5) You can seek emergency care anywhere in the US, just don't miss your renewal.
6) Insurers have to maintain a minimum medical loss ratio. Even bare-bones plans must meet this floor. Once a plan falls below compliance long enough, it gets pulled from the marketplace.
7) If you have children, they are automatically covered under your plan until age 26 regardless of employment status.
8) This is the kicker. Insurers cannot raise premiums beyond some fixed annual cap, like 3-5%. They have to justify any increase before an independent review board before it takes effect.
9) Conviction of any serious fraud by an insurer will result in immediate market removal after penalties are paid. Any minor compliance violation will prevent future marketplace participation for some number of years, like 5-10 years. Any pattern of systemic denial abuse is a permanent ban.
10) Current uninsured Americans are enrolled automatically in the public option, which means all people who have been falling through the cracks for decades would have coverage within 2-3 years. Obviously, this raises the enrollment numbers for the first few years by default. Any insurer that games the transition period faces immediate regulatory action.
11) Employers can apply to integrate their private plans with the public option framework. This will be easily abused, so has to be significantly limited in scope and requires competent oversight.
12) The Medicaid system can be absorbed into this, where an eligibility determination can be processed during annual renewals.

There are probably lots of variations on this that could work. The point is it covers a lot of Americans which helps individuals and the broader economy. It removes the predatory nature of the current system, provides incentives to encourage staying covered and staying healthy.

This isn't meant to be an implement-tomorrow plan. It probably requires too many legislative fights and at least one of our political parties to stop taking insurance industry money and start acting in good faith. It's more of a blueprint for a way to handle the too-large number of uninsured while also dealing with the economic fallout of medical bankruptcy.

I think that is an important misunderstanding between our 2 camps.  
  
When progressives talk about closing opportunity gaps—whether due to generational wealth, ZIP code, school quality, healthcare access, or neighborhood safety — it’s not about guaranteeing *equal outcomes*. It’s about ensuring a fair *starting line of the race*. Right now, too many Americans are effectively disqualified from competing in the so-called meritocracy before they even begin, through no fault of their own.

If someone is born into a wealthy household, with tutors, college-educated parents, connections, and a safe, stable environment, they’re already 10 steps ahead. That’s not a meritocracy! That’s inherited advantage. Meanwhile, a kid from a poor rural town or inner-city neighborhood might have to dodge underfunded schools, food insecurity, violence, and limited networks just to get to the same starting place.

Trying to level those barriers isn’t about handing people success — it’s about giving everyone a *real shot* to earn it through individual hard work and talent! That *is* the core of a meritocracy: that outcomes reflect effort and talent, not accident of birth.

Will perfect equality of opportunity ever exist? Probably not—it’s an ideal, not a finish line. But striving for it improves the lives of millions, expands the economy’s potential, and helps create a society that lives up to its stated values.

In short: fighting inequality of opportunity isn't “social engineering” for equality of outcome — it's the *necessary precondition* for any meaningful form of meritocracy. Otherwise, we’re just rewarding the already-advantaged and calling it fairness.

I think this is a fundamental misunderstanding between our 2 camps.

When conservatives talk about protecting individual merit and earned success — whether through personal responsibility, hard work, delayed gratification, or building strong families and communities — it's not about ignoring hardship. It's about trusting individuals to rise through genuine effort rather than government-engineered outcomes. Right now, too many Americans are being told their circumstances define their ceiling, which is its own form of disqualification.

If someone builds wealth through discipline, sacrifice, and smart decisions, their kids benefiting from that is not a flaw in the system — that's the *point* of building something. That's intergenerational responsibility! Meanwhile, decades of top-down government 'leveling' programs have poured trillions into the same broken institutions, produced the same broken results, and left the people they claimed to help even more dependent and further behind.

Protecting earned advantage isn't about rigging the game — it's about making sure effort and sacrifice actually *mean something*. Destroy the link between hard work and reward, and you don't get fairness — you get a society where nobody has a real reason to try.

Will perfect meritocracy ever exist? Probably not — but the answer isn't to drag everyone toward a government-managed median. It's to remove *government-created* barriers: overregulation, failing public school monopolies, and bureaucracies that crush upward mobility more than any inherited advantage ever could.

In short: defending earned success and individual agency isn't 'protecting privilege' — it's the *necessary foundation* for a society where striving actually matters. Otherwise, we're just punishing the productive and calling it justice.

I’m not sure exactly what prompted this question, but I’ll bite anyway.

A couple of things. First, I reject the premise that we need to rely on foreign nations for anything remotely critical or essential. The US is in the fortunate position if not really needing to rely on other countries for very much. We don’t really need military allies to defend ourselves; with two massive oceans East and West, two weak and friendly nations North and South, there are no powers which present a significant threat to the US mainland outside of a nuclear exchange. The only thing we really need military allies for is projecting power abroad, primarily by providing staging grounds for operations. But, that is far less important if the US acquiesces to a multipolar world order and shifts policy to something like the Monroe Doctrine or armed neutrality. 

Economically, there are several essential goods we don’t make here, and we should make the necessary adjustments to develop domestic suppliers and manufacturers as much as possible. For those few critical things which cannot be produced here at all, then money talks. Cut whatever deals you need to cut. America has plenty of leverage to use towards that end.

That being said, I also don’t think the US has reduced itself to pariah status like some seem to think. The US hasn’t made any military threats against its allies, at least none that I am aware of. If you are going to bring up Trump’s 51st state Canada rhetoric, just spare us both. There is no serious intention or attempt to annex Canada, this is Trump’s usual strategy of maximum rhetorical pressure until he gets a deal. 

Is the universal tariff regime good policy in my opinion? No, I don’t think it was. But, it isn’t the end of the world, either. There will be negotiations and new deals made, and this will all be water under the bridge in a few years.

Not sure what sparked this debate, but I'll weigh in.

A couple of things. First, I reject the premise that America can simply wall itself off from the rest of the world and call it strength. The US has benefited enormously from international cooperation, alliances, and trade frameworks built over decades. Pretending we can just flip a switch and go it alone is fantasy-level thinking. Our security architecture, our supply chains, our financial dominance — all of it is deeply interwoven with global partnerships. Dismantling that isn't independence, it's self-sabotage.

Economically, the idea that we can just onshore everything overnight is a fairy tale sold to people who don't understand how global manufacturing actually works. You don't rebuild semiconductor fabs or rare earth processing in a couple of years. In the meantime, consumers pay more, businesses suffer, and trading partners retaliate. That's not leverage, that's just pain with no strategy behind it.

That said, I also don't think the left needs to catastrophize every single diplomatic stumble into the collapse of Western civilization. Yes, relationships have been strained. Yes, allies are frustrated. But alliances have survived rough patches before and will again.

Do I think progressive trade policy has always been perfectly calibrated? No, honestly it hasn't. But the answer isn't retreating into isolationist nostalgia. There will be course corrections, smarter frameworks will emerge, and this moment will eventually pass.

Precedents that get shattered don't reassemble themselves. Norms that get bulldozed don't grow back like weeds. They stay gone until someone has the spine to rebuild them from scratch — and that requires a level of political will the right has historically been too timid to summon.

Just like Trump's brand of "populism" is really just a cover for his authoritarian and kleptocratic agenda, these kinds of policies act as smokescreens that obscure a broader effort to redistribute wealth to the top.

To illustrate this, let's go over Trump’s “big beautiful bill” and why it sucks.

But first, and I kid you not, Republicans have actually named the legislation “The One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” a direct nod to Trump that is so shamelessly obsequious it's nauseating.

**Tax Cuts**

Central to the bill is more than $5 trillion in tax cuts.

Republicans want to permanently extend Trump’s 2017 tax cuts that disproportionately benefited the wealthy and corporations.

To help pay for the loss in revenue, Republicans are repealing clean energy tax credits passed under Biden.

They have also proposed raising the SALT cap substantially; a controversial move that many argue reduces federal tax revenue and increases the deficit significantly. Some argue that raising the SALT cap can unfairly subsidize wealthier, high-tax states, but it can also unequally benefit rich taxpayers who are more likely to itemize their deductions.

The bill also issues a permanent exemption level of $15 million for the estate and gift tax, which primarily benefits wealthier individuals.

Republicans claim that this bill provides tax cuts for everyone, this is disingenuous. 

The tax breaks and increases in standard deductions that *might* provide some benefit to lower income, working class Americans and seniors are only temporary, while the individual rate deductions and extensions from the 2017 tax bill, along with raised exemption levels for estate taxes will remain permanent. 

In other words, while the bill may provide some tax relief for lower and middle class individuals, the majority of the tax benefits in the bill favor the wealthy and corporations.

The bill is expected to reduce federal tax revenue by roughly $4.1 trillion and it is estimated to add more than $5 trillion to the nation's deficit. The spending cuts included in the bill are *not* expected to offset these losses.

**Spending Cuts to healthcare and food assistance**

Republicans will be shifting the cost of programs like SNAP to the states and imposing work requirements for parents and older Americans applying for food assistance.

The bill requires that the states now shoulder a percentage of the cost of benefits and pay for a 50 percent increase in administrative costs.

The bill increases the age for work requirements to 64 and lowers the age a child must be for the parent to be exempt from work requirements.

The big beautiful bill includes nearly $800 billion in reduced spending for Medicaid. Republicans will be issuing new requirements for Medicaid while increasing the number of times an enrollee must verify their eligibility. The Bill also includes substantial cuts to subsidies provided by the ACA

Critics warn that these changes will cause millions of Americans to lose their healthcare and SNAP coverage.

These measures are expected to disproportionately impact lower income Americans, the disabled, seniors and children.

Republicans are also proposing restrictions on “risk coding” and marketing for Medicare Advantage plans.

Cuts here could lead to increased premiums and reduced benefits for seniors and can limit access to care, especially in underserved communities.

The bill also proposes cuts to various public health programs, which could lead to higher costs for prescription drugs and technologies.

Concerns have also been raised about a “most favored nation” prescription drug pricing model, which could limit drug availability.

**Cuts to Veterans**

The big beautiful bill includes cuts to the VA and the Toxic Exposure Fund (TEF), which covers healthcare costs for veterans exposed to toxic substances like burn pits.

**Cuts to Research**

The bill will include reductions in costs that go towards NIH funded research, which could end up halting progress on ongoing medical research projects like those focused on Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease. These cuts could disrupt developments in scientific research and innovation and lead to layoffs and fewer job opportunities in the research field.

**No taxes on gun silencers**

The bill will eliminate a $200 tax on gun silencers which has been in place since 1934. This part of the bill is backed by the NRA, shocker.

The ramifications of this are concerning as “silencers make it more difficult to recognize the sound of gunfire and locate the source of gunshots, impairing the ability of law enforcement to respond to active shooters.”

**Cuts to Planned Parenthood**

Republicans are also proposing eliminating Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood; restricting access to abortion, life saving treatments, cancer screenings, pap smears and birth control for millions of women.

**Eliminating Tax Exempt Status**

The bill will allow the Trump administration to eliminate the tax exempt status of nonprofits that support “terrorism.” Why is this bad? Because it sets an arbitrary standard and allows the Trump admin to dictate what falls under the purview of “terrorism,” meaning that it will have the power to financially cripple any charities that advocate for issues that don't align with the MAGA agenda.

**Funding for Mass Deportations**

The bill will include $46.5 billion for Trump's border wall. $4 billion to hire thousands of more immigration agents, and $2 billion for signing bonuses.

The bill also includes imposing a $1,000 fee on migrants seeking asylum.

Its stated goal is to remove 1 million immigrants per year and imprison 100,000 people in detention centers.

**Pentagon and National Security funding**

The bill includes $150 billion for the Department of Defense and provides at least $25 billion for Trump’s so-called “Golden Dome for America,” a costly and impractical missile defense shield project.

This part of the bill also includes $21 billion to restock the country’s arsenal, $34 billion to improve the naval fleet, and $5 billion more for border security.

**Taxes on Universities and Changes to Student Loans**

Republicans expect to save over $300 billion by overhauling the student loan program. This will include replacing all current loan repayment systems with plans that are far less accommodating.

The bill will eliminate Biden era regulations that made it so borrowers could cancel their loans if they were defrauded by colleges.

There will also be a 21 percent tax increase on University endowments.

**Drill, Baby Drill**

Republicans are pushing for more drilling and mining on public lands to increase revenue.

The bill allows for more leasing of public lands for drilling, mining and logging and expedites government approval for these projects.

Republicans are also cutting royalty fees once paid by companies to extract resources from the land; a Biden era measures that sought to address the effects of climate change.

While the first mRNA vaccine came from a German company (BioNTech), the collaboration with Pfizer and support from the Trump admin played a significant role in its rapid deployment. To dismiss it entirely because the research began abroad overlooks the broader context.

Regarding January 6, it was a dark day in American history, and the violence was inexcusable. That said, whether the former president legally incited the riot is still a matter of legal and public debate—there are ongoing investigations and differing interpretations of his speech and actions that day. In a country based on the rule of law, conclusions should be based on evidence and due process, not media narratives alone.

As for the term “lawfare,” it’s increasingly used to describe the perceived politicization of the legal system, where legal tools are used to achieve political ends. Dismissing it outright ignores a broader discussion happening across the political spectrum about fairness and consistency in the justice system.

Finally, calling political opponents “fascists” is not productive. Democracy is strengthened by civil discourse, differing viewpoints, and respect for the rule of law—not by demonizing those with whom we disagree. If we truly want to preserve American democracy, we need to engage in honest, thoughtful debate—not name-calling and absolutism.

While it's true that economic conditions are shaped by global forces, it's overly simplistic to claim that Republican tax cuts and deregulation had no role in widening inequality and inflating the deficit. I've already suggested, we need to agree to disagree, so I won't comment on much here, but on your last comment - your opinion of "most conservatives" may be skewed.  Some conservatives - even Trump if you consider him to be conservative - are not that deeply ingrained in the pro-life issue.  Trump is content with the issue being back to the states.  But even most pro-lifers aren't gung-ho about prosecuting the mother in cases of abortion, but prefer to focus on penalizing providers.  The mother who allows their child to be killed is often pressured into that decision by the other adults in her life (including the father), and may even be lied to about the level of development of the baby.  (It's just a "clump of cells" that happens to have fingers and toes and a heartbeat, right?).  Exceptions for rape - while not logically consistent, and often unnecessary anyway (rape may not lead to conception, and even when it does, women often choose to let the baby live), are absolutely popular among many conservatives - mostly given the rarity that this exception would really apply, and the heartbreaking circumstances involved.  Other exceptions do exist - especially medically related ones which can be logically consistent with a purely pro-life position (think: triage - saving one life instead of letting both die).

The point here is that "most conservatives", if they have a well-developed position on the pro-life issue, mostly want to curtail elective abortions, and focusing on the extreme outliers is mostly pointless unless you're trying to carve out valid exception cases.

I've already said we should agree to disagree, so I won't rehash everything, but on your last point — your characterization of 'most progressives' on abortion access is probably off base. Some liberals — even Biden if you consider him a mainstream progressive — aren't as absolutist on late-term abortion as you might think. Many Democrats are perfectly comfortable with some gestational limits. But even most pro-choicers aren't enthusiastic about unrestricted abortion up to birth, and prefer to focus on protecting early access. The woman seeking a third-trimester abortion is often in a genuinely agonizing medical situation, not making a casual lifestyle choice — and she's frequently being misrepresented by the right as some kind of monster. (It's just 'convenience,' right? Ignoring that these are almost always devastating wanted pregnancies gone wrong.) Restrictions with narrow exceptions — while not always logically consistent, and often unworkable in practice — are actually supported by many on the left, mostly given the genuine complexity of late-stage cases and the medical realities involved. Broader access protections do exist — especially for early pregnancy — which are entirely consistent with a pro-choice position grounded in bodily autonomy and privacy.

The point is that 'most progressives,' if they have a nuanced position, mostly want to protect access to early elective abortion, and fixating on extreme edge cases is mostly a distraction unless you're genuinely trying to work out where reasonable limits lie.

Well, for starters, the bill would add something like $3.8 trillion to the debt over the next 10 years according to the CBO. That alone should be a red flag to anyone who actually cares about balancing the budget or long-term economic stability. Then there’s the big increase in defense spending, pushing military budgets over a trillion. Not every conservative is on board with constantly throwing more money at the Pentagon, especially libertarians who want a more limited foreign policy.

It also rolls back a bunch of clean energy tax credits, which some folks see as just shifting favoritism back to fossil fuels instead of letting the market decide. And even though it keeps the tax cuts going, it also raises the SALT deduction cap from $10K to $40K, which mostly helps wealthier people in blue states. Not exactly populist or fiscally responsible.

On top of all that, it slashes Medicaid and food stamps (SNAP), adds stricter work requirements, and makes it harder for people to stay covered. That might sound good on paper to some, but in practice it’ll probly boot a bunch of low-income folks off the rolls without necessarily helping them find work.

And it includes a $4 trillion hike to the debt ceiling, and some weird language limiting what federal courts can do when they think parts of the bill are unconstitutional. Honestly feels like it’s trying to do way too much in one shot, and not all of it lines up with actual conservative or libertarian values.

Let's be real — this progressive wishlist would pile on trillions in new spending with zero serious plan to pay for it, according to every honest budget analysis out there. Anyone who actually cares about working families' futures should be alarmed by that alone. Then there's the bloated expansion of federal bureaucracy, creating whole new agencies and programs that will outlive their usefulness by decades and become impossible to kill. Not every Democrat is thrilled about handing that much power to Washington, especially the moderates who still believe in some limits on government reach.

It also showers subsidies on green energy cronies, which plenty of people see as picking winners and losers instead of letting innovation actually compete. And while it claims to soak the rich, the fine print is riddled with carve-outs and loopholes that mostly benefit well-connected donor class interests. Not exactly the working-class revolution it's being sold as.

On top of that, it expands entitlement eligibility in ways that strain already-stressed state budgets, removes accountability measures, and makes dependency easier to fall into than a path toward self-sufficiency. That might poll well in focus groups, but in practice it traps people in systems that don't actually lift them up.

And it hands the executive branch sweeping new regulatory authority while quietly neutering congressional oversight. Honestly feels like it's trying to ram through a generational transformation of government in one shot, and a lot of it doesn't square with what actual progressives or working-class voters say they want.

2. Ban PACs, and possibly even all political donations.  Create a federal fund to pay for campaigns.
3. Uncap the House.
4. Reinstate the fairness doctrine.
5. Make election day a national holiday.
6. Create a federal standard for voter registration.
7. Pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.
8. Pass legislation that nullifies the FBI memo stating a sitting president can't be arrested or taken to court, and put into law that no one is immune from prosecution. (This alone would have solved Trump and would discourage any other criminals who want to run for office)

If we want to get silly:

1. Abolish the Senate.
2. Place limits on free speech to guard against blatant grifters peddling political disinformation.  People love to talk about how much of a slippery slope this would be, but there's a huge gulf between banning blatant grifters knowingly spreading disinformation, and a legitimate news organization making a mistake.  
3. Change from a system where we vote for individuals to one where we vote for parties, at least at the federal level.  Federal representation should be mandated by the percentage of votes a party receives on a whole then the individual State parties would assign representatives to Congress based on the percentage of seats they won.
4. Create a new federal agency to create and manage a nation wide online voting system that would be used by all states in all elections.
5. Make voting mandatory for *everyone* older than 18, with some few exemptions that require prior authorization on an individual case-by-case basis.  Punishment should be annoying, but not overly punitive. Such as a fine based on a very low % of annual income.

There are absolutely legislative things we could have done prior to this point. Here's a short list:

1. Mandate every state must use strict voter ID laws with a federally standardized ID provided free of charge, audited by a nonpartisan board to ensure both security and access.
2. Ban corporate lobbying and revolving-door employment between regulatory agencies and the industries they oversee. No more K Street pipelines.
3. Impose strict term limits on all members of Congress.
4. Reinstate equal-time broadcast rules so no single media conglomerate can dominate political messaging.
5. Make all congressional financial disclosures real-time and publicly searchable.
6. Create a federal standard requiring all ballots be auditable with a paper trail.
7. Pass legislation codifying that federal agencies cannot be weaponized against political opponents, with criminal penalties for officials who do so.
8. Pass legislation explicitly prohibiting any president from issuing pardons to family members or former staffers — this alone would have reined in the Clinton and Biden family situations and deterred future abuse.

If we want to get silly:

2. Place hard caps on media consolidation to prevent six corporations from controlling what 90% of Americans see and hear. People love crying 'free market' but there's a massive difference between competition and a cartel.

4. Create a new independent federal auditing agency with subpoena power specifically tasked with reviewing government spending waste — fully transparent, publicly reported quarterly.
5. Require every piece of federal legislation to include a mandatory sunset clause of no more than ten years, forcing Congress to actually reauthorize laws rather than letting bloated, outdated programs metastasize forever.

To put your question back onto you, how can you determine a person simply entered the country illegally without Due Process? But what if border patrol doesn't catch them?

DEI promotes racism and - depending on what is taking place under its umbrella - it is unjustified under established Civil Rights laws.

Let's be clear: "DEI" as a label does not necessarily mean every activity and program associated with it are unethical or illegal, but it is decidedly a red flag worthy additional scrutiny.

At its core, DEI assumes the world and all institutions and systems therein are rife with discrimination; that disparities among specific demographics are evidence of this; and that the solution is engineering visible representation at the expense of merit.

For example, we have seen this for years in the corporate Diversity reporting from companies like Johnson & Johnson; American Airlines; HP; Google; and Accenture, just to name a very small few. The only way to quantify 'progress' in their DEI programs via their Diversity reporting is to measure and set percentile goals on a timeline for hiring on the basis race primarily, and gender secondarily. These quotas are demonstrably a violation of Title VII in making skin color and gender a value factor in employment and promotions.

A lack of enforcement by the EEOC and the Civil Rights arm of the DOJ has allowed this to become normal and acceptable for the better part of the last decade or more, with corporations and organizations being emboldened with the lack of consequence to keep pushing these policies as some kind of virtuous retribution for historical sins.

But then, with the 2023 Supreme Court decision striking down Affirmative Action, companies saw the writing on the wall: consequences were coming. And from there, many began divesting themselves of the DEI programs and personnel. Trump's Executive Orders gave a major boost to the situation of reminding people of the laws that have been on the books - but just under-enforced - for the last half-century.

I think Trumps EOs, and various state legislatures highlighting the term/words of DEI/Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in new legislation is counterproductive. It allows for too much legal confusion and petulant compliance. Instead, the policy should be that companies and organizations who have or are promoting DEI in their programs or activities will be audited for compliance with existing Civil Rights laws.

Voter ID and restrictive election laws promote voter suppression and — depending on what is being enacted under their umbrella — they are unjustified under established Voting Rights laws.

Let's be clear: "election integrity" as a label does not necessarily mean every measure associated with it is discriminatory or illegal, but it is decidedly a red flag worthy of additional scrutiny.

At its core, the voter suppression movement assumes elections are rife with fraud — despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary — and that the solution is engineering barriers to participation at the expense of equal access.

For example, we have seen this for years in restrictive voting legislation from states like Georgia, Texas, Florida, Wisconsin, and Arizona, just to name a very small few. The only way to quantify 'progress' in their voter suppression efforts is to measure and set increasingly narrow windows for registration, mail-in voting, and polling access — disproportionately burdening Black, Latino, and low-income voters. These restrictions are demonstrably a violation of the Voting Rights Act in making participation functionally harder based on geography and demographics.

A lack of enforcement by the DOJ Civil Rights Division has allowed this to become normalized and acceptable for the better part of the last decade, with Republican-controlled legislatures being emboldened by the gutting of Section 5 preclearance in Shelby County v. Holder to keep pushing these policies as some kind of virtuous protection against phantom fraud.

But then, with mounting court losses striking down the most egregious restrictions, legislators saw the writing on the wall — and simply got more creative. Trump's Executive Orders and MAGA-aligned state legislatures have accelerated the assault on ballot access under the cover of procedural legitimacy.

I think the piecemeal legal challenges, while necessary, are counterproductive on their own. They allow too much time for damage to be done before relief arrives. Instead, the policy should be that states enacting voting restrictions be required to demonstrate — with actual evidence — that the fraud they claim to be preventing exists at a scale that justifies the disenfranchisement they are causing.

# 1. No Congressional Authorization or Consultation

Past presidents have often sought at least some form of congressional buy-in:

* **George W. Bush** obtained full congressional authorization for the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
* **Barack Obama** launched airstrikes in Libya in 2011 without prior approval but submitted a detailed legal justification under the War Powers Resolution and consulted Congress afterward.
* **Joe Biden** ordered limited strikes in Syria and Iraq but cited existing Authorizations for Use of Military Force (AUMFs) and briefed congressional leaders.

In contrast, Trump’s Iran strike was **unilateral**, with **no prior consultation** and only a vague post-strike notification to Congress—raising red flags under both the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution.

# 2. Target and Scale

Most recent strikes targeted **non-state actors** (e.g., ISIS, al-Qaeda) or were framed as **retaliatory**. Trump’s strike hit **Iranian nuclear infrastructure**—a sovereign nation’s critical facilities—without clear evidence of an imminent threat. That’s a much more provocative and escalatory move.

# 3. Legal Justification: Preemptive vs. Imminent Threat

The U.S. has long debated the legality of **anticipatory self-defense**, but it’s controversial and not widely accepted under international law. Trump’s team leaned on **preemptive self-defense**, which is even more tenuous—striking before a threat has fully materialized. Legal scholars argue this stretches both domestic and international legal norms beyond recognition3.

# 4. International Law Violations

Unlike past actions that were at least loosely tied to UN resolutions or collective defense, this strike had **no UN Security Council authorization** and arguably violated **Article 2(4) of the UN Charter**, which prohibits the use of force against another state except in self-defense or with Security Council approval.

# 5. Lack of Transparency and Oversight

Obama and Biden both released legal memos or briefings explaining the rationale for their strikes. Trump’s administration has **withheld key intelligence** and **refused to release a legal justification**, making it harder for Congress or the public to assess the legality.

In short, this strike is seen as a **legal outlier** because it bypassed democratic checks, lacked a clear legal basis, and escalated tensions with a sovereign state without imminent provocation.
